A1.justification: Both PDFs describe R1-Code-Interpreter and the same 144-task benchmark. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support reliable comparison, including identifying material removed from v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original benchmark results for 3B/7B/14B models, training curves, and ablations, with detailed per-task results in Appendix E.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, curriculum comparisons, response analyses, and supplementary experiments in its appendices.

M1.justification: v2 adds a four-stage curriculum that ranks training samples by improvement potential estimated from 20 answers across four agent frameworks. It replaces v1's correctness-only reward with correctness, format, and turn-count terms, and raises the maximum code-call count from five to eight. These substantially change training and interaction procedures.

E1.justification: Both versions use 33 SymBench, 27 Big-Bench-Hard, and 84 Reasoning-Gym tasks, retaining the 107/37 training/held-out task division and matching task definitions. The added ablations and GPT-5 arithmetic example remain within the existing task coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds CodeSteer to the benchmark comparisons across all three model sizes, a difficulty-ranked curriculum comparator, and trained All Text/All Code comparisons. The earlier ordinary-GRPO method corresponds to the later 'wo CL' variant; Code Agent matches CI wo Fine-tune. PPO and unmasked-training comparisons are removed.

E3.justification: The reported code-call budget increases from five to eight, and v2 states that exploratory multi-turn trajectories receive greater representation in SFT. New experiments introduce four 150-step curriculum stages, matched 6.5k-trajectory SFT controls, and GPT-4o labeling of self-checking. Warm/cold-start evaluation changes from 3B/7B ordinary GRPO to 14B multi-stage GRPO.

E4.justification: v2 tests curriculum versus ordinary GRPO, potential versus difficulty ordering, and whether matched-data text/code SFT explains the gains. It adds quantified self-checking, expanded task-count sensitivity, GPU-utilization analysis, and a GPT-5 failure case. v1's PPO comparison, masking ablation, and capability radar analysis disappear; the DeepSeek/Qwen comparison is retained in the appendix.

E5.justification: v2 Figure 3d adds error bars to the task-count sensitivity analysis, whereas v1's corresponding analysis presents training trajectories without uncertainty bars. v2 does not define these bars or report their underlying repetition or seed counts, so this establishes an added reporting practice, not an increase in experimental runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 2 reports final test averages of 64.1%, 60.6%, and 51.5% for 14B/7B/3B; v2 Table 3 reports 72.4%, 66.6%, and 58.0% under revised training. These are results for changed procedures, not isolated same-setting gains. The ordinary-GRPO 14B test result also changes from 64.1% to 63.6%. New comparator and analysis results are added, while v1's detailed per-task Tables 5–7 are removed.

T1.justification: Beyond the retained RL objectives, v2 introduces the formal potential score 4p(1-p), Bernoulli reward-variance identities, policy-gradient bounds, and concentration and smoothness arguments. Sections 4.2–4.3 and Appendix C contain new lemmas, propositions, and proofs with no counterpart in v1.

C1.justification: The paper shifts from documenting limited GRPO gains to claiming that potential-guided curriculum learning overcomes that bottleneck. v2 claims superiority over GPT-4o with Code Interpreter, where v1 claimed to approach it, and introduces training-cost reduction through a CPU sandbox as a main contribution. The general-purpose integration and emergent self-checking claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 develops a sparse-reward/KL-dominance explanation for stalled GRPO and interprets curriculum ordering, late-stage saturation, and matched-SFT results. It explicitly discusses higher inference costs than single-turn textual reasoning. Conversely, v1's stated applicability limitation concerning plotting and software generation is removed, while the base-model capability limitation remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents potential estimation, stage lengths, a sandbox on five 64-core CPU nodes, and 16 rather than eight H100 GPUs. It newly states SFT/GRPO sample separation and reports 1845 GPU hours versus v1's 1600 under different procedures. However, v1's exact text/code baseline prompts, evaluation sample-count specification, checkpoint-selection criteria, and VeRL disclosure disappear. Code, data, and model access links remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds ReTool and the original chain-of-thought prompting citation, and explicitly differentiates its scope from already-cited ToRL and ToolRL. It removes the separate multi-turn SFT/RL literature paragraph and several associated references. The central positioning around general-purpose code/text reasoning across diverse tasks is retained.

P1.justification: The abstract, contributions, and conclusion are substantially rewritten around curriculum learning and execution efficiency. Training material is reorganized into a dedicated section, experiments and analysis are combined, and the appendices are substantially restructured. The title and author list also change.

P2.justification: v2 redesigns the overview and response-analysis figures, recombines training plots, expands the main comparison table, and adds curriculum, GPU-utilization, GPT-5, and SFT displays. It removes the capability radar, PPO/masking plots, and detailed per-task tables, while moving the DeepSeek table into the appendix. The document template, text width, and headers also change.

improvement.justification: Curriculum controls, matched-data SFT comparisons, and quantified self-checking provide valuable evidence absent from v1. However, v2 removes detailed results and reproducibility information, gives conflicting gain summaries in Sections 1 and 5.1, and claims a 39% cost reduction for 4500 to 1845 GPU hours, which implies 59%. Appendix C also treats maximization of a gradient upper bound as establishing maximal actual signal. These substantive benefits and losses leave the net quality direction uncertain.
